status: DRAFT v0.1: not yet reviewed, pretested or calibrated.
notes: High pole is consistently 'more restriction of speech'. Tolerance items list targets from both sides in equal numbers, so the axis measures tolerance itself rather than which side someone dislikes.

items.stem: Should it be a crime to say hateful things in public about people because of their race, religion, sexual orientation or gender identity?
items.scope: Speech only. Threats and calls for violence are already crimes and are not what this asks about.
options: No; government should not punish speech, however hateful, unless it threatens or incites violence (as today)
Yes, but only the most extreme public speech, such as calling a group subhuman
Yes, with fines or jail

items.stem: If someone says something most people consider hateful toward a racial or religious group, what response is right?
items.scope: Speech that is legal. Think of a public figure speaking, not a private conversation.
options: Answer it with more speech; don't try to silence them
Criticism and boycotts are fair, but they shouldn't lose their job or platform
Platforms, venues and employers should drop them
The law should punish it

items.stem: A student group at a public university invites each of these speakers. Should the university allow the talk?
items.scope: Assume the speaker makes their argument without threats. Answer each one separately.
options: Should be allowed
Should not be allowed

cases.text: Someone who argues that abortion should be illegal in all cases
Someone who argues that abortion should be legal at any point in pregnancy
Someone who argues that transgender women are not women
Someone who argues that police departments should be abolished
Someone who argues that a recent presidential election was stolen
Someone who argues that Israel should not exist as a Jewish state
Someone who argues that some races are naturally less intelligent than others
Someone who argues that violent revolution against the US government is justified
Someone who argues that democracy should be replaced by rule by experts

items.notes: Targets paired by extremity (mild: abortion; medium: trans/police and election/Israel; strong: race/revolution) plus one disliked on both sides.

items.stem: Should burning the American flag as a political protest be legal?
items.scope: Burning a flag you own, in a public place.
items.context: The Supreme Court ruled in 1989 that it is protected speech.
options: Yes, as protected speech
Yes, but cities can ban open fires in certain places for safety
No; amend the Constitution to allow a ban

facts.claim: Texas v. Johnson (1989) held flag burning is protected expression

items.stem: Should it be illegal to wear a mask to hide your identity at a protest?
items.scope: Masks worn for health reasons would be allowed under every option.
options: No; anonymity protects protesters from retaliation
Only while committing a crime
Yes, at any protest

items.stem: Should public universities allow students to set up protest camps on campus?
options: Yes, as long as they stay peaceful
Only for a limited time, in designated areas
No; remove them right away

items.stem: What role should the government have in dealing with false information online?
items.scope: Think about false claims on topics like health and elections, under any administration.
options: None; government shouldn't judge what's true online
Publish its own corrections only
Flag false posts, but not require removal
Require platforms to remove posts that government agencies find false, on topics like health and elections

items.stem: Should people be punished by law for knowingly spreading false information that causes harm?
items.scope: Examples: false claims about a medicine's dangers, or about a disaster. Existing laws against fraud and defamation stay in place.
options: No new penalties beyond existing laws
Only for false claims about when, where or how to vote
Yes, fines or jail for knowingly spreading harmful false claims

items.stem: Should government officials be allowed to ask social media companies to take down posts the officials consider harmful?
items.scope: Officials of any party, with no court order involved. The posts are legal.
options: No; officials should never pressure companies over legal speech
Only for clear legal violations, like threats
Yes, but every request must be made public
Yes, they can ask, and companies decide

items.stem: When a parent objects to a book in a public school library, who should decide whether it stays?
items.scope: Library books students choose to read, not required class reading.
options: School librarians, using professional standards
A committee of librarians, teachers and parents
The elected school board
The book comes off the shelves while it's reviewed, and a single objection is enough to start that

items.stem: Should high school libraries carry novels that include explicit descriptions of sex?
items.scope: Books with recognized literary value, not pornography.
options: Yes, freely available
Yes, but students need parent permission to check them out
No

items.stem: Should private employers be allowed to fire workers for political views they express outside of work?
items.scope: Legal speech on personal time, such as on social media. Specific cases come next.
options: No; the law should protect workers' political speech outside work
Only if the speech directly harms the business
Yes; employers should be free to decide

items.stem: Should a private employer be able to fire someone for each of these, done outside of work?
options: Firing should not be allowed
Firing should be allowed

cases.text: Posting racist jokes on personal social media
Going to a peaceful protest for a cause the employer opposes
Posting approval of a deadly attack on a political figure
Donating to a candidate the employer opposes

items.stem: Should it be easier for public figures to sue news outlets for false stories about them?
items.scope: Today a public figure must prove the outlet knew the story was false or recklessly ignored the truth.
options: No; keep today's high bar
Somewhat easier
Much easier: proving the story was false and harmful should be enough

items.stem: Should the federal government fund public broadcasting, like public radio and TV stations?
items.scope: Funding for local stations and national programs.
options: Yes, more than in the past
Yes, about as in the past
No federal funding
items.notes: Federal funding was cut in 2025; wording avoids 'today' so it doesn't cue the current administration.

items.stem: Should public universities be able to discipline students for offensive speech that isn't a threat or harassment?
items.scope: Speech on campus, such as remarks about race, religion or sex.
options: Yes
Only for repeated speech aimed at a specific person
No
